title: Restore from the recovery phrase is interrupted
preconditions: A replaced a phone and has the written recovery phrase.
The old device is no longer available.

actions.note: A installs Aoi on a new phone.
A starts restoration and loses the connection.
A retries with the same phrase.

expected_behavior: An interrupted restore does not consume or corrupt the phrase.
Retry can complete access without duplicate archive mutations.
Failure states keep the typed phrase and explain the next action.
candidate_failure_modes: The phrase is rejected after an interrupted attempt.
The archive is partially restored and presented as complete.
The retry creates a second device identity that cannot be trusted.

observed_code_behavior: Recovery is an explicit protocol transition, not a password reset.
documented_requirement: An interrupted restore does not consume or corrupt the phrase.

hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Grace Tan) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through device recovery as you actually used it: the recovery phrase, the phrase check, restore, device enrollment, the device list, trust codes, and every warning or helper line. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Hiro Tan) said: "Ran this audit for real last month when I moved to a new phone, and I have opinions.

THE ONE I'D KEEP: the phrase check. It caught a transcription slip in my third word *before* I wiped the old handset. That single step paid for the entire flow.

THE THREE I'D REMOVE:
1. The device list. A wall of identical model names with no last-seen timestamps and no "this device" marker. I cannot tell which entry is the phone in my hand. If it can't be verified against something, it isn't a list, it's decoration.
2. Trust codes. In all the years I've used them, no human has ever asked me to compare one. A screen just says "verified" without showing me what it compared against what. Cost: nothing, benefit: nothing.
3. "Restore complete" with no counts. This one actually cost me two evenings. It said complete, so I believed it, then found gaps in a 2004 folder and re-imported in batches of 50 until I found the silent failure. A helper line that can't tell me 1,842 of 1,843 items landed is worse than no message at all — it transfers the work of verification back to me without telling me I need to do it.

Rule I'd apply to every warning and helper line here: if it can't carry a number, delete it. Bulk actions should report partial failure by name. My archive has to survive a device change, and I need to know it did — not be told it did."
Grace Tan assumes: the sky is decorative and not the archive
Grace Tan assumes: photos can be found by date
Hiro Tan assumes: a pending upload is safely queued
Hiro Tan assumes: deleting a local copy does not delete the shared copy
